title: P102 Prevalence of insomnia and related sleep difficulties in middle childhood

sections.abstract: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title> <jats:sec> <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title> <jats:p>Insomnia and related symptoms, such as difficulty falling or staying asleep, are common in middle childhood, however, reported prevalence rates vary widely across studies.</jats:p> </jats:sec> <jats:sec> <jats:title>Objective</jats:title> <jats:p>To provide a synthesis of the prevalence of insomnia and related symptoms in children aged 6 to 11 years.</jats:p> </jats:sec> <jats:sec> <jats:title>Methods</jats:title> <jats:p>Following pre-registration, a systematic search was completed in May 2024. Studies were included if they were observational and involved community samples of children aged 6 to 11 years. Meta analyses were planned along with several subgroup and moderator analyses.</jats:p> </jats:sec> <jats:sec> <jats:title>Preliminary Results</jats:title> <jats:p>Seventy-five studies met criteria and were included (n = 173 197). Due to significant heterogeneity across studies, data are presented through narrative synthesis, with meta-analytic estimates planned where feasible. Preliminary findings revealed that prevalence rates varied widely, reflecting differences in measurement instruments, frequency thresholds, recall periods, and scoring approaches. The Sleep Disturbance Scale for Children (SDSC) and Children’s Sleep Habits Questionnaire (CSHQ) were the most commonly used questionnaires, however, inconsistent and often low thresholds were applied to define sleep difficulties. Most studies reporting insomnia focused solely on nighttime symptoms, omitting criteria such as daytime impairment and adequate sleep opportunity. Only four studies assessed insomnia based on current diagnostic criteria, with prevalence estimates ranging from 6.8% to 15%.</jats:p> </jats:sec> <jats:sec> <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title> <jats:p>These preliminary findings highlight the need for more standardised and consistent methodologies that align with diagnostic standards to improve comparability and accuracy in prevalence estimates.</jats:p> </jats:sec>
